strings.delivery.problem_p1: In the gig economy, the rider is a variable to squeeze: precarious status, no protection, earnings that keep eroding. Everyone knows it. But nothing moves, because it's the tech giants who impose their vision — and it suits their books, not people.
strings.delivery.problem_p2: We made the opposite choice: pay our riders better than anyone, here in Tours — with a clear ambition, in time: to hire them as employees, with a real contract and real protections. Not out of charity: because a fair service starts with people treated right. The only real question is how to fund it without squeezing anyone — neither your margin nor the customer. Here's the answer.
strings.delivery.problem_title: The problem no one wants to look at
strings.delivery.rule1: You set your floor margin. The minimum you're willing to make on a delivered order. It's your threshold, decided by you.
strings.delivery.rule2: Your share is capped by that threshold. It sits between your usual margin and your floor — funded by the service cost delivery saves you. We never go below your minimum.
strings.delivery.rule3: The customer pays the difference, displayed clearly at the moment of ordering. No prices quietly inflated, no hidden fees.
strings.delivery.trigger_p1: People keep saying “delivery is expensive for the resto”. Look closer. A cover in the dining room means staff to welcome, serve and clear, a table tied up for an hour. A delivered order, none of that: no table service to pay for.
strings.delivery.trigger_p2: In other words, a good part of the service cost you spend in the dining room, you don't spend on delivery. That's often where the money is to pay the person who brings the meal decently — without taking anything more off your plate.

strings.esus.p1: Captain.Food starts from a simple conviction: digital tools should serve the public good, not be a tollbooth in the hands of a few tech giants. The problem isn't that they make money — it's that once you depend on them, they can squeeze, and nothing stops them.
strings.esus.p2: So we're building in safeguards that will hold. We're aiming for accreditation as a solidarity-based social utility enterprise (ESUS, a French legal status) — a legal framework that caps profit-taking and locks in the mission — with a cooperative (SCIC) as our destination, where restaurateurs, riders and citizens will have a say. The goal: to be, by design, unable to become what we're fighting.
strings.esus.p3: And so you don't have to take our word for it: we're opening our books in public on Open Collective — every euro received and spent, meant to be visible to everyone. Radical transparency, not a slogan.
strings.esus.p4: Our horizon: for Captain.Food to be a digital commons, not a private asset. The code is open — on GitHub — under the Captain.Food Coopyleft license (a copyleft based on AGPL v3, in the spirit of CoopCycle), whose commercial use is reserved for social and solidarity economy structures — cooperatives and non-profits. Our course: getting it recognized as a digital public good (DPG) — so it's verifiable, and above all replicable: other cities, other cooperatives will be able to take it up. A tool for the common good is meant to be shared — not sold off. Read the manifesto →

strings.manifesto.anger_p1: My fight is simple: I want to build public-utility platforms, to stand up to the tech giants who abuse their position.
strings.manifesto.anger_p2: I've spent years building platforms and marketplaces. I know how they're made — and I know where they squeeze. The plight of gig-economy riders seemed like the right starting point: people grinding away, badly paid, with no protection.
strings.manifesto.anger_p3: Then I discovered the numbers on the restaurateurs' side. Commissions of 25 to 35% on every order — that shocked me. And what shocked me even more was the loss of control: restaurateurs no longer even know their own customers.
strings.manifesto.anger_p4: The math is simple. On the big platforms, a €30 dish doesn't bring you €30. It brings you about 21. The missing €9 goes out in commission, in a trade where the margin already comes down to a few points. You cook. They cash in.
strings.manifesto.anger_p5: The more I looked, the more I saw just one thing: a system where customers, restaurateurs and riders survive and complain about it — everyone, except the big platforms. So I decided to use what I know how to do — build quality software, fast — to fix a problem in society before chasing profit.
strings.manifesto.contact_band: You run a restaurant or a food truck in Tours? Write to me directly: miam@captain.food — or join the free restaurateurs. We'll talk, no commitment.
strings.manifesto.dependence_p1: We think the problem with the platforms is the commission. That's only part of it. The real problem is that your customers aren't your customers. The platform knows their name, their address, their habits. You don't. The day you leave, you start from zero.
strings.manifesto.dependence_p2: And once you depend on them, they can tighten the screw. The commission goes up? You find out. Your ranking drops? You don't know why. The rules change? You follow. You're no longer the captain of your business. You're a passenger.
strings.manifesto.dependence_title: The real problem isn't the price. It's the dependence.

There's a conviction, a legal framework, a website, and me writing to you. I'd rather tell you right away: I believe you've had enough of being told stories. So here's the real one.

strings.manifesto.offer_p2: And above all, you finally get a real home of your own online. Not a listing drowned in a giant's directory, one resto among thousands: your own site, under your own name — yourresto.captain.food, or even your own domain name yourresto.fr if you want it. Your colors, your photos, your world. A site that gets you found, that your customers remember, and that belongs to you. That's what leaving the dependence behind means: no longer renting a spot in someone else's shop window, but having your own.
strings.manifesto.offer_p3: “So what do you live on?” Good question, and the answer is here, in plain words: never on your back. The service is funded by a pay-what-you-want customer contribution — €0 is fine, no judgment — never a percentage, never on your margin, never a surcharge added for the customer.
strings.manifesto.offer_p4: And the riders: where the gig economy squeezes them into precarity, we've chosen to pay them better than anyone, here in Tours — with the ambition, in time, to hire them as employees. A fair service starts with people treated right, and we fund it without squeezing anyone (see how we pay for delivery).

strings.manifesto.refuse_p1: The temptation, when you launch an alternative, is to do the same thing but nicer at first — then squeeze once everyone is hooked. We've all seen that movie. The friendly service becomes the new tollbooth.
strings.manifesto.refuse_p2: I refuse that. Not out of kindness: by design. Captain.Food is aiming for accreditation as a solidarity-based social utility enterprise (ESUS, a French legal status). It's not a slogan: it's a legal framework that would cap our profit-taking and lock in our purpose. And our course is to become a cooperative (SCIC) — where restaurateurs, riders and citizens will have a say. The day we'd want to drift into what we're fighting, the status would stop us. It's the only safeguard worth having: not a moral promise, a rule.
strings.manifesto.refuse_p3: And so it isn't just one more promise, we're opening our books in public on Open Collective: every euro received, every euro spent, meant to be visible to everyone. The rule binds us; the books prove it to you.
strings.manifesto.refuse_p4: And I want to go even further: for Captain.Food to be a commons, not my property. The code is already open (on GitHub), under the Captain.Food Coopyleft license (a copyleft based on the AGPL, in the spirit of CoopCycle), whose commercial use is reserved for social and solidarity economy structures. And my course is to get it recognized as a digital public good (DPG) — so it's verifiable, and so another city, another band of independents, can take it up and adapt it. The result: either you inflate your online prices (and customers order less), or you swallow it (and your margin melts away). Passing the commission on doesn't cancel it — it makes your revenue pay for it.
strings.seo_nocommission.why_p2: A commission-free channel breaks that circle. An illustrative example: on a €30 order, a ~30% platform can take ~€9; with Captain.Food, it would be €0 on the dish — you keep your €30. See the funding in detail, example included →

The customer base here is loyal and local: people come back to their favourite spots. It's the ideal ground to take back control of your customer base — recover your regulars' contact details (with their consent) and bring them back, instead of depending on a platform's algorithm.
strings.seo_region.stcyr_p: On the slopes north of the Loire, a well-off, dynamic residential commune. The customer base here is demanding, attached to quality and to local business — receptive to the idea of directly supporting its restaurateurs rather than a multinational. The “money that stays close to home” angle and the customer's pay-what-you-want contribution resonate particularly well here.
strings.seo_region.stpierre_p: A railway and industrial town, shaped by the TGV station and its business zones. Food service here lives largely on the workers' lunch trade and people passing through: quick lunches, set menus, takeaway. Smooth online ordering, booked ahead and picked up with no wait, fits the local rhythm — and 0% commission clearly changes the equation on tight average tickets.
strings.seo_region.tours_p: The home port. That's exactly where a ~30% commission hurts the most, and where a direct channel under your name makes the most sense. We're launching here, with a first group of restaurateurs shaping the tool.
